page.mentor_intro: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis is not one disease but a family of them, and the antigen defines the member: bird fancier's lung, farmer's lung, hot-tub lung and the summer-type HP of humid climates each carry their own exposure pattern, clinical phenotype and prognosis. Systematic curation of reported HP-associated exposures — long missing — now underpins confident antigen identification, which remains the single most valuable diagnostic and therapeutic act in the disease, because removal of the right exposure is the only intervention that changes the natural history.

teaching_points.claim: A scoping review systematically identified reported exposures associated with HP and their clinical phenotypes, addressing the absence of curated exposure lists to inform diagnosis.

Major occupational and domestic triggers include avian antigens (pigeon, parakeet, and goose-feather bedding causing bird fancier's lung) and thermophilic actinomycetes (Saccharopolyspora rectivirgula in moldy hay causing farmer's lung).

Industrial exposure variants include isocyanate-induced HP in spray painters, metalworking fluid HP ('machine operator's lung'), and cheese washer's lung (Penicillium roqueforti), highlighting the necessity of detailed occupational histories.

Prognosis strongly correlates with specific causative antigens and host clearance: avian antigen exposure and occult domestic exposures carry higher risks of progression to irreversible pulmonary fibrosis than episodic farming antigens.

uncertainties: Many HP patients have no identifiable antigen despite systematic exposure assessment, limiting phenotype-based prognosis.
The strength of association between specific antigens and fibrotic versus non-fibrotic courses is incompletely quantified.
mcq_angles: Classic antigen-disease pairings: birds, moulds, farming dusts, hot-tub aerosols.
How antigen identification drives both diagnosis and management.
Summer-type HP and regional antigen variants.
The exposed-but-not-diseased distinction: host susceptibility factors.

page.mentor_intro: Hypertension management is the highest-yield intervention in cardiovascular medicine, and it is a moving target: the 2025 AHA/ACC guideline now retires and replaces the 2017 framework, resetting definitions, targets and treatment pathways. The through-line of modern guidance is earlier action — diagnosing with proper technique and out-of-office confirmation, starting pharmacotherapy promptly at threshold, and using combination therapy upfront for most patients — while an evidence-based update tracks the trials that shaped each change since 2017.

teaching_points.claim: The 2025 AHA/ACC guideline for the prevention, detection, evaluation and management of high blood pressure in adults retires and replaces the 2017 ACC/AHA guideline.
Important findings bearing on hypertension prevention, detection and management have accumulated since the 2017 guideline, summarised and contextualised in an evidence-based update.

First-line antihypertensive classes with proven cardiovascular morbidity and mortality reductions encompass thiazide-like diuretics (chlorthalidone, indapamide), ACE inhibitors or ARBs, and dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers.

Initial dual-combination therapy using two complementary first-line agents of different classes is recommended for patients with Stage 2 hypertension (BP >= 140/90 mmHg) or BP >20/10 mmHg over target.

uncertainties: Out-of-office confirmation logistics and white-coat versus masked hypertension management remain incompletely implemented.
How the 2025 revisions change real-world control rates versus the 2017 framework is an open implementation question.

page.mentor_intro: Blood-pressure targets are where guidelines genuinely diverge — and understanding why is more useful than memorising numbers. The American tradition targets ≤130/80 for most adults on intensive-control evidence; European guidance historically tolerated higher targets for achieved-benefit simplicity; and pragmatic primary-care frameworks like Hypertension Canada's exist because control rates regress when guidance is not implementable. An in-depth review of the 2021-era guidelines maps the concordant core (treat early, combine agents, measure properly) against the discordant edges (targets, initial combinations).

teaching_points.claim: The Hypertension Canada guideline provides pragmatic primary-care-focused recommendations to improve adult hypertension management, addressing regressing treatment and control rates.

Multiple evidence-based national and international hypertension guidelines published within four years show mostly concordant recommendations with some discordant opinions, mapped in an in-depth review.
Major international guidelines converge on recommending a target systolic blood pressure <130 mmHg and diastolic <80 mmHg for most adults with confirmed hypertension and elevated cardiovascular risk.

Out-of-office blood pressure confirmation using automated office blood pressure (AOBP), ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM), or home blood pressure monitoring (HBPM) is mandatory to rule out white-coat and masked hypertension.

uncertainties: Whether the intensive <130/80 target generalises to all subgroups outside trial populations is debated.
How to operationalise individualised targets in routine practice is unresolved across guidelines.
mcq_angles: US versus European target philosophy and its trial underpinnings.
The concordant core across guidelines: measurement, combination therapy, adherence.
Primary-care implementation frameworks and control-rate realities.

page.mentor_intro: How low to drive blood pressure is hypertension's defining controversy. Intensive control — the ≤130/80 philosophy — has trial evidence for cardiovascular protection, but its net clinical benefit varies by target and patient characteristics, and benefit-harm trade-off analyses now quantify what guidelines assert. The counterpoint literature reminds us the optimal target remains undefined, that more intense therapy carries hypotension, renal and electrolyte costs, and that 'lower is better' is a population claim that needs individual calibration at the bedside.

teaching_points.claim: Although intensive blood pressure control is recommended by major guidelines, its overall benefit-harm balance remains uncertain; net clinical benefit varies by blood pressure target and patient characteristics.

The optimal target blood pressure is undefined and controversial; recent American guidelines recommend ≤130/80 mm Hg for essentially all adults, while more intense versus standard therapy trade-offs continue to be debated.

Intensive systolic blood pressure lowering (target <120 mmHg vs <140 mmHg) significantly reduces major adverse cardiovascular events and all-cause mortality in high-risk non-diabetic adults (SPRINT trial).

Intensive therapy requires close surveillance for predictable adverse effects, including asymptomatic serum creatinine rise, orthostatic hypotension, syncope, and electrolyte disturbances (hypokalemia, hyponatremia).

uncertainties: The harms threshold — at what achieved BP hypotension-related events offset cardiovascular gains — differs by frailty and age.
Real-world adherence to intensive targets is substantially worse than trial conditions, diluting population benefit.
mcq_angles: SPRINT-style intensive-control evidence and its generalisability.

page.mentor_intro: Treating hypertension in the very elderly is where the evidence-based and the humane can collide. Systolic hypertension dominates as arteries stiffen, and trial data support treatment well into the ninth decade — but frailty, orthostasis, polypharmacy and limited life expectancy all argue for targets individualised beyond the population guideline. The Cochrage update on higher targets found the major trials aimed at modest systolic goals and demonstrated cardiovascular benefit, while frailty-focused guidance stresses standing pressures, deprescribing review and shared decision-making over rigid numbers.

teaching_points.claim: Arterial hypertension prevalence rises with age, mainly systolic hypertension from arterial stiffening, and chronic elevation remains a major cardiovascular risk factor in older populations.
A Cochrane update found that most major antihypertensive trials in adults 65 and older targeted systolic BP below 160 mmHg and collectively demonstrated cardiovascular benefit.
Clinical trials published in 2020–2021 address hypertension onset age, risk and treatment questions relevant to older adults, summarised in a dedicated trials update.

uncertainties: Whether the intensive <130 target extends to the frail very elderly without harm is unresolved by trial evidence.
Optimal deprescribing thresholds when standing BP falls or falls risk escalates are judgement-based.

page.mentor_intro: Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy — chronic hypertension, gestational hypertension and pre-eclampsia — are among the leading causes of maternal and perinatal mortality worldwide, complicating a substantial share of pregnancies. Modern management rests on accurate classification, because each category carries different risks, surveillance intensity and delivery timing. The 2021 ISSHP recommendations and ACOG Practice Bulletin 222 define the framework: low-dose aspirin for prevention in high-risk women, magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis, and delivery as the definitive treatment for pre-eclampsia at term or when maternal status deteriorates.

teaching_points.claim: Hypertensive disorders are a leading cause of maternal and perinatal mortality; pre-eclampsia complicates 2–8% of pregnancies globally.
ISSHP 2021 recommendations cover classification, diagnosis and management of hypertensive pregnancy disorders, with uniform departmental protocols and outcome audits advised for all managing units.
Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy include chronic hypertension, gestational hypertension and pre-eclampsia; new developments include early-pregnancy screening to identify women at high risk.

page.mentor_intro: Pre-eclampsia is a life-threatening, uniquely human disease of pregnancy and a leading cause of maternal and neonatal morbidity and mortality — with consequences that outlast delivery, since survivors carry increased lifetime risks of stroke, cardiovascular disease and diabetes. The modern paradigm has shifted upstream: first-trimester combined screening (maternal factors, blood pressure, uterine-artery Doppler, biomarkers) to identify high-risk women, and low-dose aspirin started by 16 weeks to prevent early-onset disease, the subtype with the worst outcomes.

teaching_points.claim: Pre-eclampsia is a leading cause of maternal and neonatal morbidity and mortality; survivors have reduced life expectancy with increased risks of stroke, cardiovascular disease and diabetes.

Early-onset pre-eclampsia requiring preterm delivery carries higher complication risks, and low-dose aspirin initiated before 16 weeks reduces pre-eclampsia in high-risk women identified by first-trimester screening.
Hypertensive disorders complicate approximately 16% of pregnancies in the United States, and low-dose aspirin initiation by 16 weeks reduces pre-eclampsia in high-risk women.

uncertainties: Which screening algorithm performs best in different populations is still being optimised.
Post-partum cardiovascular risk-reduction strategies for pre-eclampsia survivors are not yet formalised.

page.mentor_intro: A hypertensive emergency is not a number — it is acute blood-pressure rise with new or worsening end-organ damage, and everything follows from identifying the damaged organ: encephalopathy, intracranial haemorrhage, acute coronary syndrome, pulmonary oedema, or acute kidney injury. Management is deliberately heterogeneous and agent-matched: labetalol, nicardipine, esmolol, glyceryl trinitrate and sodium nitroprusside each fit specific organ scenarios, and the goal is controlled, partial reduction — typically around 20–25% in the first hours — because normalising pressure too fast steals cerebral and coronary perfusion. Malignant hypertension, defined by retinal haemorrhages or exudates with acute renal deterioration, is the phenotype that most often reaches the ICU.

teaching_points.claim: A hypertensive crisis is a sudden, significant BP rise to 180/120 mmHg or higher and is a medical emergency capable of causing heart attack, stroke and other life-threatening problems; management strategies are evaluated in a systematic review.

Patients with hypertensive emergencies, malignant hypertension and acute severe hypertension are managed heterogeneously; initiating therapy and setting acute BP goals requires scenario-specific considerations, per the British and Irish Hypertension Society.
Malignant hypertension is defined by bilateral retinal haemorrhages or exudates, with or without papilloedema, plus acute heart failure and acute deterioration in renal function.

uncertainties: The ideal first-line IV agent by clinical scenario remains partly institution- and resource-dependent.
Precise BP-reduction targets in each end-organ emergency vary across position documents.
mcq_angles: Emergency versus urgency distinction and the end-organ survey.

page.mentor_intro: Hypertensive nephrosclerosis — nephroangiosclerosis — is the kidney disease that accompanies chronic essential hypertension, known for over a century and still diagnosed more by clinical context than by biopsy, which is reserved for doubtful or atypical cases. The clinical picture is one of slowly progressive chronic kidney disease with subnephrotic proteinuria in a patient with long-standing, often poorly controlled hypertension. The modern nuance is that the causal arrow is not always simple: some 'hypertensive' nephrosclerosis may reflect primary renal microvascular disease driving the hypertension rather than vice versa, particularly in certain ancestries.

teaching_points.claim: Nephroangiosclerosis — kidney disease accompanying chronic essential hypertension — has been recognised for over a century; definitive diagnosis is by renal biopsy, reserved for doubtful or atypical cases.

Pathologically, chronic arteriolosclerosis is characterized by medial hypertrophy, intimal hyalinosis of afferent arterioles, and downstream ischemic glomerulosclerosis, leading to progressive non-proteinuric or subnephrotic renal decline.

High-risk APOL1 genetic variants (G1 and G2 alleles) strongly predispose individuals of African ancestry to accelerated hypertensive nephrosclerosis and aggressive progression toward end-stage renal disease.

Blood pressure control targeting <130/80 mmHg using RAAS inhibitors (ACE inhibitors or ARBs) combined with lifestyle sodium restriction (<2 g/day) represents the cornerstone of secondary renal protection.

uncertainties: The bidirectionality question — whether renal microvascular disease precedes hypertension in some patients — is unresolved.
Whether aggressive BP control halts established nephrosclerosis beyond general CKD benefit is inferred rather than proven.
mcq_angles: Clinical diagnostic pattern: CKD plus chronic hypertension plus subnephrotic proteinuria.
When biopsy is indicated (atypical features, active urinary sediment).
Differential: other secondary hypertension causes with renal involvement.
Management as CKD with strict BP control and renin-angiotensin blockade.

page.mentor_intro: Hyperthyroidism is common — roughly 0.2–1.4% of people worldwide — and its management rewards precise diagnosis because the aetiology dictates the treatment. Overt disease is biochemically defined by suppressed TSH with elevated free T4 and/or T3; beyond that, the thyrotoxicosis work-up separates true hyperthyroidism (Graves' disease, toxic nodular goitre — hormone overproduction) from thyroiditis (hormone leak), using TRAb, uptake scanning and clinical signs such as orbitopathy. Each pathway has distinct therapy: antithyroid drugs, radioiodine, surgery, or simply time and beta-blockade.

teaching_points.claim: Overt hyperthyroidism — suppressed TSH with high T3 and/or free T4 — affects approximately 0.2% to 1.4% of people worldwide; subclinical disease is defined by low TSH with normal hormone levels.
Clinical suspicion should be confirmed biochemically (low TSH, high FT4 or FT3), with a global prevalence of 0.2–1.3%.
Hyperthyroidism refers to increased hormone synthesis and secretion, most commonly from Graves' disease or toxic nodular goitre, whereas thyroiditis causes thyrotoxicosis through hormone leak.

uncertainties: Antithyroid-drug duration, relapse prediction and the long-term Graves' management pathway vary by guideline and patient factors.
Management of subclinical hyperthyroidism, particularly in older adults, is individualised.

Graves' versus toxic nodular versus thyroiditis differentiation.
